4,800 tribal students, with the condition that the State Government would
ensure 100 per cent placement of the trainees and would select an
implementing agency by observing transparent procedure and relevant
financial rules“. However, approval of implementing agency (Acetel), as
proposed by State Government, was conveyed by Gol on 9 June 2011. The
grant (® 9.36 crore) received from Gol was transferred (January 2012) by the
department to personal deposit account of Commissioner, TAD, Udaipur, for
implementation of the programme.

On a presentation made by Acetel Technologies (July 2011) before the
department, the Commissioner observed (August 2011) more shortcomings 6
in it and proposed to State Government for selection of agency through open
tenders to ensure transparency. The State Government also noticed (February
2012) that the procedure adopted for selecting the implementing agency
(Acetel) was not clear and transparent and therefore cancelled all its financial
sanctions and revoked orders of conducting the said training through Acetel.
The unspent grant was initially deposited in government treasury which was
finally adjusted by Gol against the subsequent grants to State Government
under SCA to TSP.

Thus, selection of agency without following proper procedure led to
cancellation and revoking of the training programme and non-utilisation of
special central assistance of € 9.36 crore by the State Government.

Admitting (March 2014) the facts of cancellation of the training programme
due to selection of Acetel without following a transparent procedure, the
department argued that there was no financial irregularity as the funds were
not misutilised. The reply was not acceptable as cancellation and revoking of
the training programme resulted in non-utilisation of हैं 9.36 crore and
deprivation of tribal students from job opportunities.

Cost per student was more than रैं 19500/; condition of advance payment; placement of
only 10 per cent of students; lack of district wise targets; period of training not specified
etc.

“ As per item No. 9 of Appendix VII A of Rule 306A of the Public Works Financial &
Accounts Rules, selection process of hiring consultancy services include (i) approval of
the Finance Department; (ii) preparation of terms of reference; (iii) preparation of cost
estimates; (iv) advertisement; (v) short listing of consultants; (vi) evaluation etc.

Training proposed for students of 10" class and above while their experience was for
training engineering students only; possibility of higher drop rates for students of 10"
class; less chance of employment of trained students as they would be below 18 years;
agency asked for ashram hostels or residential schools for training which were not
available; presentation lacked manner of training and amount required; placement of only
10 per cent of students.

The Finance Department issued (November 2004) instructions for conducting
four Audit Committee Meetings per year. Only 36 Audit Committee meetings

taken against the defaulting officials and recoveries of losses/outstanding
advances/ overpayments are made in a time bound manner.

Executive Summary



This Audit Report has been prepared in six chapters. Chapters I to V deal with Social,
General, Economic, Public Sector Undertakings, Revenue Sectors and Chapter VI deals
with Follow up of Audit observations.

This Report contains 28 audit paragraphs (including sixteen general paragraphs) and four
Performance Audits. According to the existing arrangements, copies of the draft
compliance audit paragraphs and draft performance audits were sent to the Secretary of
the Department concerned by the Principal Accountant General (Audit) with a request to
furnish replies within six weeks. Replies were received from the departments concerned
except in respect of five paragraphs.

Expenditure of हैं 4.21 crore was rendered infructuous due to improper survey and

injudicious selection of site for the construction of 575 bedded hospital.
(Paragraph 1.3)

Violation of guidelines resulted in irregular expenditure of % 6.48 crore due to excess
deployment of 648 teachers in schools while other schools faced shortage.
(Paragraph 1.4)

Government of India (GOI) introduced (March 2005) Rajiv Gandhi Grameen
Vidyutikaran Yojana with the objective of providing access to electricity to all Rural
Households and improving the rural electricity infrastructure. 90 per cent of the overall
cost of the projects was to be provided by GOI as capital subsidy. The balance project
cost was to be met by the Governments of respective States through loan from Rural
Electrification Corporation Limited. Cost of electrification of BPL households was,
however, to be subsidised fully by the GOI. Energy and Power Department, Government
of Sikkim was the implementing agency of the scheme in the State.

Under the scheme, the State targeted to electrify 25 un-electrified villages and intensive
electrification of 413 already electrified villages with free electricity connection to 12,081
BPL households by March 2009. The projects could not be completed even after four and
half years of scheduled completion time. As of November 2013 the EPD completed
electrification of all 25 un-electrified villages as well as intensive electrification of 383
villages which were already electrified and provided free electricity connection to 9,832
BPL households.

(Paragraph 2.3)



Concerned with the slow growth in the Agriculture and allied sectors, the National
Development Council in its meeting held on 29 May 2007, resolved to launch a special
Additional Central Assistance Scheme Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) to
incentivise States to draw up plans for their agriculture sector more comprehensively.
RKVY aimed at achieving four per cent annual growth in the Agriculture sector during
the XI Plan period by ensuring a holistic development of Agriculture and allied sectors.
The main objectives of the scheme inter alia were: (i) to incentivise the States so as to
increase public investment in Agriculture and allied sectors; (ii) to achieve the goal of
reducing the yield gaps in important crops, through focused interventions; (iii) to bring
about quantifiable changes in the production and productivity of various components of
Agriculture and allied sectors by addressing them in a holistic manner.

In Sikkim, the Agriculture and allied sector had achieved four per cent annual growth rate
towards contribution to Gross State Domestic Product during the XI Plan period.
However, adequate and envisaged planning process for overall vision for development of
the district was absent both in the District Agriculture Plan and State Agriculture Plan
and it was coupled with flaws in the preparation of DPRs. Failure on the part of the Nodal
Department to furnish the UCs in time also led to the curtailment of funds. In cases of
production of major crops (i.e. Cereals, Pulses and Oil seeds), the four per cent growth
rate was achieved only in two years.

The smooth functioning of the scheme and achievement of its objectives was adversely
affected by improper fund management, delays, taking up of unviable projects and lack of
monitoring, review, evaluation and field studies from the State Level Selection
Committee.

(Paragraph 2.4)

Audit of ‘Execution of Suspension Foot Bridges (SFBs) under SIDF’ by the Rural
Management & Development Department through Zilla Panchayats revealed that out of
66 SFBs, 51 were completed and remaining 15 were under construction. Out of the
completed SFBs, 21 SFBs were completed recording a delay of more than six months.
The results of Audit on implementation of projects indicated defective survey and
estimation, irregularity in award of works, execution of works inconsistent with
technically sanctioned approved designs and estimates, excess and avoidable expenditure
on construction of SFBs with longer span than required, undue favour to contractors,
excess issue of material and unauthorised expenditure.

(Paragraph 2.5)

The Department violated the terms of sanction of the Government of India which resulted
in unauthorised expenditure of 92.40 lakh.
(Paragraph 2.6)



Unauthorised expenditure of = 187.08 lakh under Integrated Nutrient Management due
to non-adherence to cost norms as stipulated under the guidelines of the scheme.
(Paragraph 2.7)

Contractors were paid हें 1.97 crore for carriage of stones which was in excess of
requirement as stipulated in the AOR and in violation of the SPW Manual
(Paragraph 2.8)

Rejection of the highest offer for sale of power (30 MW) by the Energy and Power
Department without valid reason resulted in loss of € 2.55 crore besides loss of interest of
% 1.01 crore against unrecovered sale proceeds of € 7.14 crore.

(Paragraph 2.9)

Due to failure in insisting upon the Bank for honouring the Bank Guarantee in full, the
Company could not recover हैं 1.28 crore causing interest loss of € 51 lakh.
(Paragraph 3.2)

Levying of interest beyond the permissible limit by the Company resulted in extra
financial burden of € 38.64 lakh on the beneficiaries.
(Paragraph 3.3)

Delay in assessment of tax for the period 2006-07 to 2010-11 on sales turnover of
% 142.80 crore benefitted a company as it retained tax collected from the consumers
amounting to हैं 28.56 crore over a period exceeding two to seven years.

(Paragraph 4.5)

Irregular utilisation of Way Bills resulted in evasion of SVAT amounting to % 1.09 crore.
(Paragraph 4.6)

Systemic lacunae in the Commercial Taxes Division to ensure realisation of taxes from
works contractors executing works of registered dealers resulted in loss of revenue of
% 38.21 lakh.

(Paragraph 4.7)



The Audit on Disaster Management indicated that the State, despite being located in a
seismically active zone and being a victim of recurrent natural disasters, was yet to
adequately recognise these disasters as threats which thwarted its developmental plans
and mission to transform itself into a model State within a targeted time frame. The
Disaster Management Act 2005 and other guidelines issued by the GOI from time to time
covering all issues of Disaster Management (DM) had not been implemented fully. The
institutional mechanism to address DM issues had not been firmly established and the
DM policy 2007 not fully implemented. Further, the State DM plans require
strengthening and the Departmental DM plans were not made till the date of audit
(September 2013). There had been diversion from funds provided by GOI for immediate
relief and long-term reconstruction of damaged infrastructure.

The lack of urgency to address the issue of disasters is underscored by the fact that even
after more than seven years of enactment of the DM Act 2005 by the GOI, the State had
not laid down a proper institutional framework with appropriate manpower having
designated roles and responsibilities to address DM in the State. The apex body, State
DM Authority (SDMA) met only once during the five year period 2008-13, that too, only
to discuss relief activities after the earthquake of 18 September 2011. DM had not been
incorporated in the development planning process of the State. No financial resources had.
been earmarked in the State’s Plan towards DM. The State entirely depended on Central
support both for immediate relief activities as well as permanent reconstruction of
damaged infrastructure.

However, after the earthquake of 18 September 2011, the Government has initiated
various policy resolutions and capacity building measures which were expected to
strengthen DM in the State.

(Paragraph 5.3)

Sikkim became part of North East Region in April 1998 and availed the benefit of
funding from NLCPR and NEC. A number of infrastructural projects were constructed
out of these funds in various sectors such as Roads & Bridges, Irrigation & Flood
Control, Energy & Power, Human Resource Development Department, etc. The overall
responsibility of managing NLCPR and NEC funds is primarily vested with the
Development Planning, Economic Reforms and North Eastern Council Affairs
Department. The projects relating to Roads & Bridges are implemented by Roads &
Bridges Department.

The Audit of Roads & Bridges projects funded under NLCPR and NEC for the period
2008-13 was carried out during July-August 2013. The results of audit disclosed that out



of a total of 44 projects, only 18 (41 per cent) were completed. None of the projects were
completed within the scheduled dates. The physical progress of incomplete projects
ranged between 11 and 98 per cent as of March 2013. The completed projects (18) also
recorded a delay in completion ranging between one and 12 years beyond the scheduled
date of completion. This was partly due to delayed initiation of tender procedure,
defective preparation of DPRs, frequent change in scope of works, cost revision, short
release of matching share by State Government, etc. Similarly, out of total funds of
% 246.91 crore released during 2008-13, ~ 218.03 crore was incurred during 2008-13. Out
of = 218.03 crore spent, irregular and excess expenditure of = 19.27 crore were noticed in
Audit. The unspent funds coupled with irregular excess expenditure and slow pace of
implementation of projects indicated that the speedy development of infrastructure
projects was not achieved to the desired extent.

(Paragraph 5.4)

Audit process starts with the assessment of risks faced by various departments of
Government based on expenditure incurred, criticality/complexity of activities, level of
delegated financial powers, assessment of overall internal controls, etc.

After completion of audit of each unit on a test check basis, Inspection Reports containing
audit findings are issued to the heads of the departments. The departments are to furnish
replies to the audit findings within one month of receipt of the Inspection Reports.
Whenever replies are received, audit findings are either settled based on reply/action
taken or further action is required by the auditee for compliance. Some of the important
audit observations arising out of these Inspection Reports are processed for inclusion in
the Audit Reports, which are submitted to the Governor of the State under Article 151 of
the Constitution of India for laying on the table of the Legislature.

The test audits were conducted involving expenditure of % 686.52 crore (including
expenditure of ~ 374.05 crore of previous years) (details of year-wise break-up is given
in Appendix 1.1) of the State Government under Social Sector. This Chapter contains
two Compliance Audit Paragraphs as given below:



For upgradation and modernisation of Sir Thutob Namgyal Memorial (STNM) Hospital,
Gangtok, the Health Care, Human Services & Family Welfare Department invited
(January 2008) ‘expression of interest’ from various firms of which five firms responded.
This was done without calling for tenders or through advertisement. The detailed
‘expression of interest’ submitted by these five firms were scrutinised by the Department
and M/s Archtech Consultants Private Limited (ACPL), Kolkata was selected (May 2008)
on the basis of recommendations of the Technical Committee constituted (April 2008) for
this purpose. The ACPL was entrusted with the preparation of Detailed Project Report
(DPR) along with Architectural Structure and Services Designing for 500 bedded Multi
Speciality Hospital at STNM complex, with the approval (May 2008) of the Cabinet.
The agreement was signed (June 2008) with the firm for the above works at a total fee of
% 6 crore (six per cent of the initial indicative project cost of € 100 crore).

Subsequently, the project at STNM complex was cancelled on the ground of insufficiency
of space and a revised proposal of the Department for consturction of a 575 bedded Multi
Speciality Hospital at Sokeythang (Tadong), through Building and Housing Department
(BHD), was approved (August 2008) by the Cabinet. Without calling for tenders, a
corrigendum to the agreement with ACPL was issued (March 2009) for preparation of

Audit process starts with the assessment of risks faced by various departments of
Government based on expenditure incurred, criticality/complexity of activities. level of
delegated financial powers, assessment of overall internal controls, etc.

After completion of audit of each unit on a test check basis, Inspection Reports containing
audit findings are issued to the heads of the departments. The departments are to furnish
replies to the audit findings within one month of receipt of the Inspection Reports.
Whenever replies are received, audit findings are either settled based on reply/action
taken or further action is required by the auditee for compliance. Some of the important
audit observations arising out of these Inspection Reports are processed for inclusion in
the Audit Reports, which are submitted to the Governor of the State under Article 151 of
the Constitution of India for laying on the table of the Legislature.

The test audits were conducted involving expenditure of = 1,166.34 crore (including
expenditure of ¥ 633.58 crore of previous years) (details of year-wise break-up is given in
Appendix 2.1) of the State Government under Economic Sector. This Chapter contains
one Performance Audit on ‘Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana’ and five Compliance Audit
Paragraphs as given below:

Government of India (GOI) introduced (March 2005) Rajiv Gandhi Grameen
Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) with the objective of providing access to electricity to all
Rural Households (RHHs) and improving the rural electricity infrastructure. Ninety per
cent of the overall cost of the projects was to be provided by GOI as capital subsidy. The
balance project cost was to be met by the Governments of respective States through loan
from REC. Cost of electrification of BPL households was, however, to be subsidised fully



by the GOI. Energy and Power Department, Government of Sikkim was the implementing
agency of the scheme in the State.

Under the scheme, the State targeted to electrify 25 un-electrified villages and intensive
electrification of 413 already electrified villages with free electricity connection to 12,081
BPL households by March 2009. The projects could not be completed even after four and
a half years of scheduled completion time. As of November 2013, the EPD completed
electrification of all 25 un-electrified villages as well as intensive electrification of 383
villages which were already electrified and provided free electricity connection to 9,832
BPL households.

2.3.1.1 Electrification is regarded as a vital necessity for the development of rural areas.
Hence, rural electrification has been a key component of various development schemes.
As per Rural Electrification Programme (2003-04) of Government of India (GOI),
definition of village electrification was revised (February 2004). According to the revised
definition, a village would be declared electrified if basic infrastructures such as
distribution transformer and distribution lines are provided in the inhabited locality;



electricity is provided to public places like schools, panchayat offices, health centres,
dispensaries, community centres, etc.; and, the number of households electrified should
be at least 10 per cent of the total number of households in the village.

The National Electricity Policy formulated (February 2005) by the GOI inter alia States
that the key objective of the development of the power sector is to supply electricity to all
areas including rural areas as mandated under Section 6 of the Electricity Act, 2003. Both
the GOI and the State Governments would jointly endeavour to achieve this objective.
GOI introduced (March 2005) Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY)
with the objective of providing access to electricity to all Rural Households (RHHs) and.
improving the rural electricity infrastructure. The scheme was to be implemented during
2005-2009 (by March 2009) under the 10" and 117 plan periods (viz., 2002-07 and
2007-12) with the following objectives:

» establishing the Rural Electricity Distribution Backbone by providing 33/11KV
(or 66/11KV) Power Sub Stations (PSS) of adequate capacity;

v

creation of Village Electrification Infrastructure i.e., electrification! of un-
electrified villages/habitations and provision of distribution transformers of
appropriate capacity;

> catering to the requirement of electricity for agriculture and other activities
including irrigation pump sets, small and medium industries, healthcare,
education, etc. to facilitate overall rural development, employment generation and
poverty alleviation; and

Vv

electrification of un-electrified Below Poverty Line (BPL) households with 100
per cent capital subsidy.

2.3.1.2. Rural Electrification Corporation Limited (REC) was the nodal agency for

State level Rural Electrification Plan

2.3.3.1. The MoP, GOI notified (August 2006) the Rural Electrification Policy with the
aim of providing access to electricity to all households by the year 2009. As per the Rural
Electrification Policy, the State Governments need to prepare and notify a Rural
Electrification Plan (RE Plan) within six months of notification of the Rural
Electrification Policy (viz. by February 2007). The requirement of notifying the RE plan
by State Governments in consultation with MoP was reiterated in the office memorandum
(OM) issued (February 2008) by MoP, GOI on sanction of continuation of RGGVY in the
11" Five year plan. The RE Plan was to be the roadmap for generation, transmission,
sub-transmission and distribution of electricity in a State so as to ensure achievement of
the objectives of the scheme within the stipulated time frame. As per the said OM of
MoP, in case the RE plan of any State is not notified within the stipulated period, the
capital subsidy provided under the scheme was to be converted into interest bearing loan.
MoP issued (April 2008) draft template for RE plan which included plans to energise
villages being electrified under RGGVY and strengthening of sub-transmission system to
cater to additional load after electrification of villages.

Excluding total interest income of & 3.91 crore earned by EPD against investment of scheme funds during 2008-09 to 2012-13
(viz. 70.13 crore in 2008-09, 70.21 crore in 2009-10, 70.14 crore in 2010-11, 71.60 crore in 2011-12 and @ 1.83 crore in

2012-13).



It was observed that the EPD could submit (January 2012) the draft RE Plan after a delay
of 60 months from the date (February 2007) stipulated under Rural Electrification Policy.
The draft RE Plan was, however, not approved by MoP as it failed to cover several
important aspects like upgrading of sub-transmission and transmission system, investment
plan, provision of revenue subsidy by State, etc. EPD revised the RE Plan and re-
submitted the same in October 2012. The revised RE Plan was, however, pending for
approval by MoP (November 2013).

Thus, in absence of approved RE Plan, the State could not ensure development of
adequate rural electricity infrastructure. Further, failure to notify RE plan exposed the
EPD against the risk of capital subsidy being converted into loan under RGGVY.

EPD stated (August 2013) that RE plan was submitted to REC during 2007 and was
rejected on the ground that it did not cover entire rural areas of the State. The RE Plan
was re-submitted (October 2012) to MoP for approval and same was yet to be received
(November 2013).

The reply is contrary to the facts as draft RE plan was originally submitted to MoP only
in January 2012 and EPD could not provide documents in support of their contention.
Failure to notify RE Plan had led to non-completion of the project even after seven years
of sanction (December 2006) of the Scheme (November 2013).

Formulation of RGGVY Scheme and preparation of DPR

2.3.3.2 For implementation of the Scheme in the State, a Bipartite Agreement was
executed (August 2005) between REC and EPD. Under the agreement, responsibility for
project formulation and its implementation in the identified areas involving planning,
design, engineering and procurement was entrusted to the EPD.

As per the directives of GOI, EPD was required to submit the Detailed Project Reports
(DPRs) in respect of four Districts of Sikkim to GOI by September 2005. EPD could,
however, submit (March 2006) the DPRs after a delay of six months, which were
approved in December 2006. The delay in submission of DPRs by EPD was attributable
mainly to late submission of basic data by the field offices.

Scrutiny of records revealed (May 2013) that the DPRs prepared by EPD had several
deficiencies as discussed below:

> Though the electricity connections to rural households were partially proposed to be
given out of the existing infrastructure, no assessment of the spare capacity
available with the existing infrastructure was conducted. Further, no estimates were
prepared to determine the quantum of additional energy required to cater to the
needs of the new connections (BPL and APL households proposed). Thus, the DPRs
were prepared without exhaustive field survey so as to identify the surplus
infrastructure available and actual energy requirements.

> The DPRs considered electrification of 64 out of 123 un-electrified schools. The



remaining 59 un-electrified schools were omitted to be covered under the RGGVY
scheme in the DPRs due to improper survey.

v

Based on the criteria laid down in Tenth Five-Year Plan (2002-2007), Department
of Economics, Statistics, Monitoring & Evaluation (DESME), GOS, had listed out
(October 2010) 21,618 households under BPL category in the State. The DPRs
prepared by EPD, however, reckoned total number of BPL households in the State
of Sikkim as 34,784 which was higher by 61 per cent of the BPL households as
identified by DESME.

» Subsequent revisions in the number of eligible BPL Households as well as the
quantum of work involved indicated that the initial DPRs were not realistic and
were prepared without proper field survey.

The above deficiencies in the DPRs ultimately led to inadequate provision of
infrastructure for rural power supply and shortfall in achieving 100 per cent village
electrification within the scheduled period.

EPD replied (August 2013) that DPRs were prepared based on field survey by the
departmental engineers and the methodology adopted for selection of BPL households
was as per the recommendations of the panchayats duly authorised by the Block
Development Officers concerned. It was further stated that all un-electrified schools were
proposed for coverage under the Scheme.

The reply does not adequately address the issue of adopting higher figures of BPL
households without reconciling the differences with the figures available with GoS. Since
the Government already had an official list of BPL households, the same should have
been adopted for implementation of the scheme. As regards electrification of schools, the
documents available with audit confirm that 59 out of 123 un-electrified schools remained.
out of the RGGVY coverage.

Absence of Business Plan and Financial Analysis

2.3.3.3 As per the guidelines prescribed by REC, the DPR should contain the Business
Plan and Financial Analysis of the project providing the category-wise details about
anticipated number of consumers, connected load, anticipated sale of energy, operation
and maintenance expenses, etc. for the next 15 years of operation so as to evaluate
sustainability of the proposed project. The DPRs submitted by the EPD did not, however,
contain any such Business Plan and Financial Analysis. Hence, in absence of Business
Plan, EPD failed to properly assess the additional energy requirement against the
infrastructure created under RGGVY and its revenue sustainability.

EPD stated (August 2013) that being a Government Department, they were not required
to formulate a Business Plan. The reply is contrary to the requirements of the REC project
formulation guidelines which prescribed for submission of Business Plan and Financial
Analysis by the project implementing agency with complete details of projected cash
inflow and outflow for next 15 years.



2.3.3.4 For the implementation of RGGVY Scheme in the State, the EPD bifurcated the
work into two parts, viz., (i) execution of electrification works upto Low Tension (LT)
distribution pole; and (ii) providing of connections from LT distribution pole to BPL
households. The works of electrification upto the LT distribution pole was executed
through turnkey contractors whereas the works of providing of connection from
distribution pole to BPL Households was executed by EPD departmentally.

2.3.3.5 For execution of works upto the LT distribution pole through tumkey
contractors, the entire scheme in the State was divided into eight packages” under four
districts and awarded to the lowest bidders after inviting open tenders at an aggregate cost
of % 178.11 crore®. As per the Letter of Award (LoA), the contractors were to complete
the work within 18 months of award of work. The package wise details of the work, value
of the contract (pre-quantity variation), actual cost and time taken are detailed in
Appendix 2.3.1.

It could be seen from the Appendix that out of the eight packages scheduled for
completion by August 2010, only three packages could be completed as of November
2013 after delays ranging from 9 months to 15 months. Remaining five packages were
pending for completion (November 2013) even after delay of 39 months from the
scheduled date. Delays in execution of packages by the contractors correspondingly
contributed towards delay in overall implementation of the Scheme in the State.

Reasons for the delay in completion of works are discussed in the succeeding paragraphs.

Surveys and submission of quantity variation proposal

2.3.3.6 As per the RGGVY milestones set by MoP, detailed surveys to assess
requirement of quantities against sanctioned scheme works were to be completed within
six months of award (February 2009) of work i.e., by August 2009. Due to delay in
conducting surveys, EPD could submit (November 2010) quantity variation proposal after
a delay of 14 months. The quantity variation proposal was, however, approved by GOI
after taking further period of 14 months in February 2012 at an estimated cost of हैं 47.63
crore as detailed in Appendix 2.3.2. EPD took another six months in issuing (August -

Concerned with the slow growth in the Agriculture and allied sectors, the National
Development Council (NDC), in its meeting held on 29 May 2007, resolved to launch a
special Additional Central Assistance Scheme Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) to
incentivise States to draw up plans for their agriculture sector more comprehensively.
This would involve a new scheme for Additional Central Assistance to State Plans,
administered by the Union Ministry of Agriculture over and above its existing Centrally
Sponsored Schemes, to supplement the State-specific strategies including special schemes
for beneficiaries of land reforms. Thus, RKVY aimed at achieving four per cent annual
growth in the Agriculture sector during the XI Plan period, by ensuring a holistic
development of Agriculture and allied sectors. The main objectives of the scheme inter
alia were:

(i) to incentivise the States so as to increase public investment in Agriculture and allied
sectors; (ii) to achieve the goal of reducing the yield gaps in important crops, through
focused interventions; (iii) to bring about quantifiable changes in the production and
productivity of various components of Agriculture and allied sectors by addressing them
in a holistic manner.

In Sikkim, the Agriculture and allied sector had achieved four per cent annual growth
rate towards contribution to Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) during the XI Plan
period. However, in cases of production of major crops (i.e. Cereals, Pulses and Oil
seeds), the four per cent growth rate was achieved only in two years (2008-09 and
2011-12 for Cereals and Pulses and 2009-10 and 2011-12 for Oil seeds) of the period
under review.

Adequate and envisaged planning process for overall vision for development of the
district was absent both in the District Agriculture Plan (DAP) and State Agriculture
Plan (SAP) and it was compounded with flaws in the preparation of DPRs. As a result,
the gaps in various agricultural initiatives remained unidentified and the improvement in
the production of agricultural products was also not achieved. Even the financial targets
set by the Department were unrealistic and highly inflated.



The smooth functioning of the scheme and achievement of its objectives was adversely
affected by improper fund management, delays, taking up of unviable projects and lack of
monitoring, review, evaluation and field studies from the State Level Selection Committee

(SLSC).

Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RK VY) was launched with the aim of achieving four per
cent annual growth in the Agricultural sector during the XI Plan period by ensuring
holistic development of Agriculture and allied sectors with the objectives to incentivise
the State to invest on Agriculture sector, maximise profits to the farmers, bring about
quantifiable change in the production ete.

The funds under the scheme were provided to States as 100 per cent grant by the Central
Government. The eligibility for assistance under the scheme would depend upon the
amount provided in State Plan Budget for Agriculture and allied sectors, over and above
the base line percentage expenditure™ incurred by the State Governments on Agriculture
and allied sectors. The State would ensure that the baseline share of agriculture in its total
State Plan expenditure (excluding the assistance under the RKVY) is at least maintained,
and upon its doing so, it would be able to access the RKVY funds.

The RKVY would be available to the States in two distinct streams i.e. at least 75 per
cent of the allocated amount under Stream I for specific projects and the balance amount
would be available under Stream II for strengthening the existing State sector schemes
and filling the resource gaps. A State Level Sanctioning Committee (SLSC), constituted,
would have the authority to sanction specific projects under Stream I.

24.7.1

Preparation and submission of District Agriculture Plan (DAP)/State
Agriculture Plan (SAP).

According to the guidelines of RKVY, each district would formulate DAP by including
the resources available under various existing schemes (i.e. District, State, or Central
schemes, etc.) and adhere to the guidelines circulated by the Planning Commission for
District Planning. The DAP would present the vision for Agriculture and allied sectors
within the overall development perspective of the district and would present the financial
requirement and the sources of financing for the agriculture development plans in a
comprehensive way. The objective of district planning was to design an integrated and
participatory action plan for the development of the local area in general and Agriculture



and allied sectors in particular. For projecting the actual requirements for development of
Agriculture and allied sectors of the district, the planning process was to be initiated from
the grass root level ie. at village/Gram Panchayat Level. The Nodal Department was to
ensure that the State’s priorities with respect to Agriculture and allied sectors are
appropriately captured in the DAPs. After preparation of the DAPs, the Nodal
Department would finalise the comprehensive SAP by integrating all the DAPs. After the
approval of SAP, the Nodal Department would place the Stream I proposals before the
SLSC for consideration, discussion, finalisation, and sanction.

Scrutiny of DAPs and SAP revealed that there was no reference to the on-going
schemes/programmes (other than the RKVY projects) in the SAP and DAPs and that
merely the names of other on-going schemes (Appendix 2.4.1) were provided in the
DAPs. Scrutiny of the SAP and DAPs also indicated that the Department had not taken
any step to explore and identify the possibility of convergence of RKVY with other
existing schemes/projects. Hence, the DAPs and SAP could not adequately integrate
resources available from different sources with RKVY which was an objective of the
scheme. The shelf of projects at district level was not prepared. Documents in support of
the initiation of the planning process from village/GP level though called for, was not
produced to Audit. The DAPs were prepared without considering the overall resources
available for development of Agriculture and allied sectors and also without any inputs
from the village/GP level. The DAPs and SAP appeared to be mainly an exercise to
obtain funds from GOI.

Records regarding the submission of SAP and DAPs to the DAC and Development
Planning, Economic Reforms & North Eastern Council Affairs Department
(DPERNECAD) of State Government were not produced to Audit.

Thus, adequate and well-envisaged planning process for overall vision for development of
the district was absent in the DAPs. The flaws in the preparation of SAP and DAPs
resulted in non-viable projects being taken up, irregular implementation of projects and
non- improvement in agricultural production, as elaborated in the succeeding paragraphs.
2.4.7.2 Detailed Project Report

Detailed Project Report (DPR) is a basic document for planning and implementing a
project. The DPR is to be prepared carefully and with sufficient details of the project to
ensure its appraisal and implementation in an economical and efficient manner. In a well-
prepared project, all the essential ingredients would be properly considered and included,
i.e. feasibility studies, competencies of the implementing agencies, anticipated benefits to
the farmers, definite time-lines for implementation, etc. The Nodal Agency would satisfy
itself that the project fulfilled the objectives of the RKVY before recommending the
DPRs to the SLSC.

Audit observed that the DPRs were prepared by the implementing departments without
proper surveys and investigations and lacked the essential inputs. The Nodal Department
had submitted these DPRs to the SLSC without proper verification. Details of
shortcomings in the DPRs are given below:



> Project on Baby Corn, Sweet Corn and Pop corn:
The DPR was prepared taking into consideration only the input cost and without any
market survey. The selling price, earning and availability of market, etc. were not
spelt out in the DPR. This resulted in the implementation of a non-viable project as
detailed in Paragraph 2.4.10.1.
> Establishment of Feed unit at Melli Payong:

The SLSC approved the establishment of Feed unit at Melli Payong at a total cost of
% 1.21 crore scheduled to be completed by 31 March 2013. The project was being
implemented by Food Security and Agriculture Development Department (FSADD).
Scrutiny of records revealed that the DPR only stated the financial aspect of the
project and did not quantify the benefit that was to be delivered to the farmers. The
current market price of feed and the selling price of feed from proposed unit were not
taken into consideration for calculating detailed benefits (cost benefit ratio) that was
to be delivered to the farmers. Moreover, the feasibility study was also not
conducted. Due to the inherent defects in the DPR, the project was not taken up even
after two years of sanction. Even after inviting the offer by the Department for
construction and operation of the project, only two agencies responded to the bids,
one of which offered very low rate and another offered bids without any supporting
documents and rate. After obtaining the approval, the Department again appointed a
firm for preparation of Project Report at a total cost of = 6 lakh which indicated that
the initial DPR was prepared without proper scrutiny by the Nodal Department.

> Packing house for fruits and Flowers:
The DPR had detailed the expenditure on the construction of the infrastructure only,
that too, without taking into account the requirement of a packing house. The
benefits that were to be delivered to the farmers and its impact on agricultural
production were not specified in the DPR.

> Establishment of Piggery farm at Melli Dara:
Establishment of Piggery farm at Melli Dara at a total cost of = 90.67 lakh was
approved by SLSC in October 2009. The project was being implemented by
AHLFVSD. The work was awarded to the contractor at par to be completed within
June 2010. After the payment (October 2010) of the first running bill, the scope of
work was changed (February 2011) and a new estimate was framed (April 2011) for
% 1.19 crore. This validated the fact that the initial DPR was prepared without proper
survey and investigation. Due to the improper preparation of the DPR, the project
remained incomplete even after a lapse of more than three years from the date of
approval by SLSC.

The Department while accepting (November 2013) the audit contention stated that the

2.4.13.1 Monitoring and evaluation by Nodal Department
As per the guidelines, the SLSC would inter-alia be responsible for:
a) Monitoring the progress of the sanctioned projects/schemes;

b) Reviewing the implementation of the scheme’s objectives and ensuring that the
programmes are implemented in accordance with the guidelines laid down;

c) Commissioning/undertaking field studies to monitor the implementation of the
projects;

d) Initiating evaluation studies from time to time, as may be required;

e) Undertaking any other project of importance to the State’s Agriculture and allied
sectors.

In Sikkim, the SLSC was constituted in December 2007 and was required to hold

meetings once a quarter. Scrutiny of records revealed that during 2007-13, as against the

required 20 meetings, only 6 meetings had been held, which resulted in shortfall of 14

meetings, thereby affecting effectiveness in the implementation and monitoring of the

RKVY as required. Scrutiny of the minutes of the meetings made available to audit also

revealed that no discussion was held on issues like the status of projects, reasons for

delay in progress of work, or whether objectives of the Scheme were being met, etc. The

SLSC while sanctioning projects, made some recommendations in those six meetings

which were partially followed up as detailed in Appendix 2.4.2.

Physical and financial performance/achievements were not monitored with reference to
the targets and objectives of the projects which resulted in delay in completion of
projects, irregular implementation, non—achievement of objective of the projects, non-
viable projects being taken up etc. Further, the lack of monitoring was also reflected in
poor record keeping on the part of both the Nodal and implementing departments.



> Field inspection:
No field inspection was undertaken by the SLSC or by the officers of the Nodal

Department to monitor the implementation of various schemes for taking remedial
action to rectify the shortcomings when detected.

> Submission of quarterly physical and financial progress reports to the Union
ministry:

Effective monitoring of any programme depends mainly on timely submission of
reports and returns to the monitoring authorities. However, the implementing
Departments failed to submit any progress reports to the Nodal Department. The
Nodal Department consequently failed to submit the performance report in terms
of physical and financial achievements as well as outcomes to the Union Ministry.

2.4.14.1 Agrarian status of the State

The net cultivated area of Sikkim is around 79,000 hectare. Since Sikkim is a hilly State,
the agriculture scenario is dominated by soil acidity, excess moisture during monsoon
period and moisture stress during post monsoon/winter, heavy weed infestation, low
temperature stress during winter, occurrence of hailstorm in pre kharif season and
incessant rain that causes leaching of nutrients and pesticides which favours high
incidence of diseases and pests that reduce crop yields. The main strength of the State is
its diverse climate for production of different quality of sub tropical to temperate fruits,
vegetables and flowers. The horticultural produce has high market potential in domestic
and distant markets.

The State Government has put forth a policy of organic farming with the target of making
Sikkim an Organic State by 2015. The Government framed organic action plan in the year
2003 and constituted the Sikkim State Organic Board.

2.4.14.7 Evaluation

No evaluation on the implementation of the programmes and their impact on the State
were conducted either by the State Government or by any independent agency. Thus,
effectiveness of the programmes and their impact on the State was not assessed.



The planning process for the implementation of the scheme was not effective and failed to
address the basic requirement of convergence of various schemes for overall development
of the Districts. The DPRs were prepared without proper survey, investigation, market
study etc. Failure on the part of the Nodal Department to furnish the UCs in time also led
to the curtailment of funds. Large sums of advance remained unadjusted for a
considerable period. Projects were characterised by delay in implementation, overlapping
of the projects and implementation of non-viable projects. Monitoring was not in place
and evaluation was also not conducted. The State maintained the four per cent growth in
agricultural sector but the production of major crops had declined.

» Projects should be implemented as per the approval of SLSC and with the

and to take corrective measures in case of any deviations; and

Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoONER), Government of India (GOI)
accorded administrative approval and financial sanction (February 2010) of % 29.71 crore
for ‘Construction of 66 Suspension Foot Bridges (SFBs)’ in Sikkim under Social &
Infrastructure Development Fund (SIDF) as part of = 500 crore package announced
(February 2008) for North East Region during 2008-09. The project was implemented by
the Rural Management and Development Department (RMDD), Government of Sikkim
through Zilla Panchayats (ZPs). As of March 2013, 51 SFBs (out of 66) were completed
and remaining 15 were under construction. Out of 51 SFBs completed, 21 were belatedly



completed recording a delay of more than six months (6-12 months- 6 SFBs; and beyond
1 year- 15 SFBs).

Thematic Audit of SFB under SIDF was taken up with the objective to assess whether the
selection of projects were need based and projects were implemented with due regard to
economy, efficiency and effectiveness. A total of 16 (out of 66) bridges were selected for
detailed scrutiny based on two stage sampling by adopting ‘Stratified’ and ‘Monetary
Unit Sampling’. The sample was later increased to 27 for increased assurance. Audit was
conducted during April- June 2013 through visits to the sites and test check of records.
maintained at the RMDD headquarters office, Gangtok and four Zilla Panchayats in the
districts.

The performance were benchmarked against the criteria stipulated in Sikkim Public
Works Code and Manual, terms and conditions set forth in the Administrative approval
and sanction orders by the DoNER, ete.

The audit findings are enumerated in the succeeding paragraphs:
2.5.3.1 Funds Management

A total of = 29.12 crore was released by DoNER of which expenditure of = 25.12 crore
was incurred upto March 2013, leaving an unspent balance of € 4 crore as shown below:

% 29.12 crore received from DoNER between March 2010 to December 2011 were kept

Government. As a result, terms of sanction of DoNER was violated. Besides, this entailed
a loss of = 76.79 lakh on account of opportunity cost of interest on savings accounts even
when calculated at a low interest rate of four per cent per annum as detailed in Appendix
2.5.1 (a), (b), (०) and (d).



The Department stated (October 2013) that loss calculated by audit was presumptive, as
keeping the funds under budget head did not affect the progress of the work and even the
XIII Finance Commission recommendation discourages keeping the funds outside the
consolidated fund of the State. The reply was not acceptable as the funds were released by
DoNER and the Department was supposed to comply with the terms and conditions of
financial sanction set by the DoNER. It was also noticed in audit that the funds received
under other Programmes (Total Sanitation Campaign etc.) were kept in separate bank
accounts. On one hand, the Department had violated instruction of the funding agency by
giving reference of the XIII Finance Commission Report and on the other hand, it
continued to keep the funds in separate bank account for other schemes.

> Unauthorised expenditure

The terms of sanction (Para 3 (x)) by the DoNER stipulated (February 2010) that the
funds should be utilised strictly for the purpose for which they were sanctioned and that
no diversion of funds would be permitted.

Audit noticed that the implementing Department unauthorisedly utilised = 25.75 lakh
towards contingency in excess of the approved amount. Against the approved
contingency funds of % 50.78 lakh, the Department incurred हैं 76.54 lakh resulting in an
excess expenditure of = 25.75 lakh which was without any authorisation from the funding
agency.

The Department stated (October 2013) that their record indicated expenditure of 47.07
lakh was incurred from the contingency funds which was not acceptable as the figures
were without any supporting documents and also the Utilisation Certificate submitted to
DoNER showed an expenditure of € 76.54 from contingency funds.

2.5.3.2 Avoidable expenditure

Sikkim Public Works Manual (Para 4.1 read with 4.5) envisaged that the estimate of the
projects must inter-alia contain history indicating initiation and reasons leading to the
proposal, design indicating a description of the original proposals and those finally
adopted particularly with regard to location, setting and design specifications and
drawings. Hence, survey forms a vital component of the estimate of projects, especially
that of SFBs.

Audit noticed that although the original estimate was based on actual requirement and
detailed survey for identification of proper site, the assessment of span of the bridges
were inflated to obtain maximum assistance from the DoNER under SIDF. The following
cases will illustrate the points:

> SFB at Lower Borong

The SFB at Lower Borong was approved (February 2010) at an estimated cost of 91.26
lakh by DoNER with the objective of providing rural connectivity. According to the
technically approved estimate, the SFB over Rangit river at Lower Borong was to have
140 mtrs. span. The departmental engineer however informed (14 June 2010) that the site
was suitable for 105 mtrs. span and not 140 mtrs. as reflected in the approved estimate.



The field engineer was directed (18 June 2010) to locate an alternative site and submit
fresh proposal. Accordingly, fresh survey was conducted (22 June 2010) for search of
alternative site to accommodate 140 mtrs. Span. Physical verification revealed that the
bridge was constructed at a different site than originally approved.

> SFB at Dhargaon Phamtam

In case of Dhargaon Phamtam also, the 150 mtrs. span SFB was administratively
approved (February 2010) at an estimated cost of हैं 94.76 lakh to provide rural
connectivity. According to the field engineers, the site identified was suitable (21 June
2010) for 65 mtrs. span rather than 150 mtrs. span reflected in the approved estimate. The
field engineer was directed (21 June 2010) to identify alternative site to accommodate
150 mtrs. span SFB. Based on this direction, alternative site was located (25 June 2010) at
a distance of 50 mtrs downstream of the original site. Accordingly, the SFB was
constructed at an alternative site to accommodate 150 mtrs. span.

This not only indicated the defective assessment of length of span required but also
execution of the bridges at the site other than what was originally identified by the
Department and approved by the DoNER. The proposal for a span length, which was.
more than the actual length required at the proposed site, resulted in unnecessary
avoidable expenditure of % 36.97 lakh on construction of two bridges as detailed in
Appendix 2.5.2. Those extra funds expended could have been gainfully utilised
elsewhere to obtain maximum benefit in furtherance of SIDF objectives.

The Department stated (October 2013) that the field officials were instructed to re-verify
the site of construction and stick to the original site as far as possible. The instruction was
issued on the concept that the sanctioned scheme did not get diverted from the original
demand. The reply corroborates the audit observation as the spans in the original sites
were shorter than the spans of the bridges at changed sites.

2.5.3.3 Unauthorised expenditure

Terms of sanction (Para-3 (x)) stipulated that the funds would be incurred towards
specific projects and no diversion would be allowed. It was, however, noticed that the
approved span and site of the projects were altered without obtaining approval of the
funding agency (DoNER) as detailed below:

> SFB at Chuba in South Sikkim

The estimate of SFB over Kalej Khola at Chuba in South Sikkim was sanctioned
(February 2010) for € 33.08 lakh for 65 mtrs. span. The subsequent survey (June 2010) on.
receipt of sanction intimation revealed that the site was suitable for 25 mtrs. span and not
65 mtrs. span. The Department, however, constructed the SFB of 65 mtrs. span over
Bhutey Khola (instead of Kalej Khola) at an estimated cost of दैं 33.08 lakh (expenditure
₹ 29.66 lakh till date) without obtaining approval of DoNER. This led to unauthorised
expenditure of € 29.66 lakh (total committed expenditure हैं 33.08 lakh for the project) as
of March 2013.



> SFB over Rangit at Tokal

The ‘Construction of 145 mtrs. SFB over Rangit at Tokal’ was tendered (29 July 2010)
and awarded (5 January 2011) to the lowest bidder at 14.5 per cent above the estimated
cost with the condition for completing within twelve months (by January 2012).

Audit noticed that the span of the bridge was revised from 145 mtrs. to 100 mtrs. due to
change of location of the bridge which was not intimated to DoNER. The Department
misled the DoNER as the work order to the contractor and the Progress Report to the
DoNER continued to mention the earlier site and span (145 mtrs.).

This led to unauthorised expenditure of हैं 39.15 lakh (total committed expenditure of
% 1.31 crore for the project) as of March 2013. Though both the estimates were framed on
the basis of the same SOR (i.e. SOR 2006), the change in span of bridge from 145 mtrs to
100 mtrs had decreased the estimate of the bridge component by only हैं 599, Audit
analysis revealed that the estimate for 100 mtrs span was inflated by हैं 15.42 lakh as
detailed in Appendix 2.5.3.

The Department reiterated (October 2013) that the field officials were instructed to re-
verify the site of construction and stick to the original site as far as possible. The
instruction was issued on the concept that the sanctioned scheme did not get diverted
from the original demand. However, the fact remains that the original site was changed
without obtaining approval from the funding agency. Further, the Department had not
spelt out any reasons for inflated estimate of SFB over River Rangit at Tokal.

2.5.3.4 Tendering and award of works

The terms of sanction (Para-3(ii)) by DoNER envisaged (February 2010) that the State
Government ensure competitive bidding through wide publicity in the print media and in
the web site. The same was reiterated in the fund release orders as well.

Audit noticed that the Department did not comply with the terms of the sanction and
instead awarded works to Co-operative Societies in contravention to the above
stipulations.

The Department expressed their regret (October 2013) for not obtaining approval from

GOI before cancelling the competitive bidding as it would take long time to get approval
from GOI.

2.5.3.5 Excess expenditure on works

Sikkim Public Works Manual (Para-19.25) envisaged recovery of excess materials issued
to the contractors at double the issue rate.

Physical verification of 27 SFBs by Audit jointly with departmental officers revealed that
excess materials were i:

sued to the contractors. Joint physical verification and audit
analysis revealed that various items such as chequered plate (95 nos.), cross beams (65
nos.), and long beams (173 nos.) were issued in excess of what was actually utilised by
the contractors. The cost of the excess materials was recovered at normal issue rate (as



against the requirement of double the issue rate) leading to undue favour to the
contractors amounting to हैं 24.13 lakh (₹ 4.30 lakh towards fitting and fixing of excess
materials and % 19.84 lakh towards the recovery of cost of materials) as detailed in
Appendix 2.5.4,

The Department stated (October 2013) that the requirement of the bridge components
calculated in the estimate was unreasonably high due to presence of bugs in the software
“Yellow Jacket’ developed and used for preparing estimates of materials for the bridges.
Further, the Department stated that during the process of construction, some of the
materials get wasted which has to be considered as fait-accompli and is unavoidable.

The reply is not tenable as the estimates, though prepared by software was approved in
hardcopy and the same could have been checked. Moreover, undue favour was given to
the contractor by making payment for the works that was not executed at all. Further, the
Department failed to explain reasons for not recovering the cost of materials issued in
excess of requirement.

2.5.3.6 Execution of works

Sikkim Public Works Manual (Para- 4.17) provides that the design and drawings of the

cable is always 1.5 mtrs. above the railing.

According to the technically approved estimate, long beams were required to be placed in

of bridges by the audit team along with the departmental officers revealed (July 2013)
that long beams in two bridges were placed in two lines (instead of three) as shown

This led to construction of bridges in deviation from the originally approved design and
also compromised safety standards besides incurring payment on account of materials
(₹ 1.51 lakh) which were not utilised.

In agreeing to the observation, the Department stated (October 2013) that the technical
manpower employed for the work do not have every detailed knowledge on the
construction of suspension foot bridges and the same has to be considered a fait-accompli.

Audit of ‘Execution of Suspension Foot Bridges under SIDF’ by the Rural Management
& Development Department through ZPs revealed that out of 66 SFBs, 51 were
completed and remaining 15 were under construction. Out of the completed SFBs,
21 SFBs were completed recording a delay of more than six months. The results of Audit
on implementation of projects indicated defective survey and estimation, irregularity in
award of works, execution of works inconsistent with technically sanctioned approved
designs and estimates, excess and avoidable expenditure on construction of SFBs with
longer span than required, undue favour to contractors, excess issue of materials and
unauthorised expenditure.

The following are the recommendations for further improving the implementation of the
SFBs under SDF:

> The survey and investigation mechanism may be strengthened to ensure minimal
change in the estimate after obtaining approval and sanction of funds from GOI;



> Selection of site may be done only after proper site verification to ensure
execution of appropriate span and design;

> Financial management may be strengthened to avoid undue favour to the
contractors; and

> Ensure utilisation of the required materials in the execution of projects to ensure

safety and adherence to approved design.

Analysis of Rates (AOR) is prepared by the Roads and Bridges Department (RBD) for
settling the rates for various items of works executed by the works departments. The
AORs also stipulate the (i) specification and the quantity of materials required to be used
in various items of works and (ii) deduction of 20 per cent of stone derived from the
excavation/hill cutting of hard/blasting rocks as usable stones for which stacking charges
@ हैं 7.02 per cubic metre was also allowed. Further, Sikkim Public Works (SPW)
Manual (Clause 45) stipulates that the contractor is required to submit all the
permits/royalty documents in original as proof of transportation of materials from the
designated quarry.

Scrutiny (February-March 2013) of the bills and statements of theoretical consumption
related to utilisation of stones during April 2008 to March 2013 pertaining to 14 works
revealed that payments to the contractors on account of carriage of stone were released by
the Department on the basis of quantity of stones claimed to have been utilised by the
contractors, without considering the quantities permissible as per the AOR. The
Department had not cross checked the quantity of stones required to be used as per the
specification in the AOR by taking into consideration the availability of 20 per cent of
stone from hard/blasting rock.

Moreover, it was seen that the contractors had not submitted the transit/royalty documents
as proof that the materials had actually been transported, to support the claim of the
quantity of stones transported, as required under the SPW Manual.

Audit observed that the actual requirement of stones to be transported was 84,246.65
cubic metre. Against this, the Department made payment for carriage of 1,20,995.30
cubic metre of stones. This resulted in excess payment of हैं 1.97 crore for the stated
transportation of 36,748.65 cubic metre of stones, which was over and above the quantity
required for the works, as per the AOR. Details are given in the Appendix 2.8.1.



Thus, failure on the part of the Department in exercising due diligence while checking the
quantum of stones for which payment was admissible, and also not taking into account
the 20 per cent derived from the cutting/hardblasting of usable stones as stipulated in the
AOR norms and ignoring the requirements of the SPW Manual, resulted in giving undue
benefit of € 1.97 crore to the contractors.

‘The matter was reported to the Department/Government (July 2013); their reply had not
been received (October 2013).

Bank Guarantee (BG) is an instrument issued by Banks in which they agree to stand
guarantee against non-performance of a party and as per the stipulated conditions of BG,
the issuing Bank shall compensate the beneficiary to the extent of the guaranteed amount.
As per directions (July 2007) of Reserve Bank of India, payment should be made to the
beneficiary on invocation of BG without delay and demur.

Government of Sikkim awarded (September 2004) the work of “Fabrication & Erection
pertaining to Water Conductor System, Penstock pipes and allied works” of Rellichu
Hydro Electric Power Project (HEP) to M/S Yuksom Engineering Works Pvt. Ltd
(Yuksom) at a cost of € 9.58 crore. The work was required to be completed within two
years (September 2006. Subsequently, the development of the Rellichu HEP was handed
over (November 2005) to Sikkim Power Development Corporation Limited (Company).

The Company released (February 2006) mobilisation advance of % 2.30 crore to Yoksom.
for supply of material against BG of State Bank of Sikkim (SBS) for हैं 2.35 crore. The
BG was valid for one year (viz. upto 3 February 2007), which was renewed by Yuksom
for a further period of one year only (viz. upto 4 February 2008). The BG was not
renewed thereafter.

Scrutiny of records revealed that Yuksom did not execute the work even after a lapse of
three years from the date of issue of Work Order. The Company, therefore, invoked
(1 February 2008) the BG before its expiry (viz. 4 February 2008) and requested SBS to
deposit the amount released against BG in the Fixed Deposit for a period of one year.
Against the BG of % 2.35 crore, however, SBS released (February 2008) ₹ 75 lakh only
which was invested in Fixed Deposit. A further sum of = 27 lakh (March 2011) was
adjusted towards the pending bills of the contractor. Although the BG of 2.35 crore was
to be immediately honoured by the bank, the Company failed to follow up and insist upon.
the SBS for fulfilling its obligation and release balance amount of & 1.28 crore. As a
result, the balance unrecovered amount of mobilisation advance (21.28 crore) has not
been received by the Company till date (May 2013).



Considering the huge loan burden of the Company, the project relating to the
development of Rellichu HEP was also abandoned as per the decision (August 2009) of
the Board of Directors of the Company.

Thus, inaction on the part of the Company to pursue with SBS for release of balance
amount of BG invoked (February 2008) resulted in non-recovery of € 1.28 crore for more
than five years causing loss of interest of = 51 lakh (at eight per cent for five years).

In reply, the Management accepted the facts and stated (July 2013) that the efforts are
being made to recover the balance amount of mobilisation advance.

The matter was reported (June 2013) to Government; their replies had not been received
(October 2013).

Department, Govt. of Sikkim with the main objective to provide financial assistance to
the eligible beneficiaries belonging to Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST) &
Other Backward Classes (OBC) whose annual income was less than 31,592 per annum

The Company is the State Channelising Agency (SCA) for financing the income

Section 11(2) of Sikkim Sales Tax Act 1983 read with Rule 12 (1,2 and 4) of Sikkim
Sales Tax Rules 1983 required mandatory submission of quarterly returns alongwith the
proof of payments by the dealers within 30 days following the quarter (30 April, 31 July,
31 October and 31 January of every year).

Test check (February 2013) of records of Commercial Taxes Division revealed that one
dealer i.e., M/s Mount Distilleries had not been assessed for local sales tax (LST) for the
period from April 2006 to March 2010. The Division issued demand notice after
provisionally assessing (April 2011) the tax liability of the said dealer for हैं 7.71 crore on
a turnover of € 77.11 crore. Audit scrutiny of the said assessment revealed the following
irregularities:

> The tax liability was calculated at the rate of 10 per cent of the gross sales
turnover instead of applicable 20 per cent. It was done presuming, without
verification that the dealer had claimed for eligibility of tax benefit for having
gone for expansion.

v

Assessment was done after deducting हैं 32.53 crore from gross sales turnover
as cash discount. Sikkim Sales Tax Act 1983 defines ‘sale price’ as the
amount payable towards the sale of goods, less any sum allowed as ‘cash
discount’ by the seller to the buyer. Other types of discounts like turnover
discount, target discount, sales promotion discount, etc. are not eligible for
deduction from the sale price.

Scrutiny revealed that the said amount was not eligible to be treated as cash discount as

the same was not granted through the invoice/bill at the time of sale of goods. The
Division had admitted the discount as cash discount only on the basis of dealer’s

? LST of 10 per cent is applicable for the industrial units eligible for incentives under the Industrial Policy Scheme

of the Government. Other units including M/s Mount Distilleries are liable to pay LST @ 20 per cent.



statement without verifying the documents in support of any cash discount. In absence of
any record with the Division in support of ‘cash discount’, requisition for documents was
issued to Excise Department. However, no such document could be produced by that
Department too.

After these being pointed out (February 2013) in Audit, the Division made (March 2013)
final assessment at the rate 20 per cent of gross sales turnover and disallowing the ‘cash
discount’ earlier admitted in provisional assessment. The turnover was, therefore,
enhanced to = 142.80 crore and the tax liability assessed for = 28.56 crore.

The Division stated (August 2013) that it had issued the demand notice for the said
amount and penalty (€ 14.28 crore). It was further stated that the dealer has filed
application for review of the assessment and has raised objection on the imposition of
full rate of tax and penalty, which was under examination.

While the tax due has not been realised and is under review (October 2013), fact remains
that the company was not assessed for the period 2006-07 to 2010-11, before 8 March
2013, thereby extending the undue benefit to the dealer of retention of the tax amount of
र₹ 28.56 crore collected by him over a period of two to seven years as detailed in
Appendix 4.1.

46 Non-evy of Sikkim Value Added Tax
According to Section 2 (xxxvi) of the Sikkim Value Added Tax (SVAT) Act 2005,
taxable turnover means the turnover on which a dealer is liable to pay tax as determined
after making such deductions from his total turnover and in such manner as may be
prescribed. Under Section 2 (vii), capital goods which are exempted from tax liability,
means plant, machinery, dyes, tools and equipment used in the process of manufacturing,
excluding civil structures and such goods as may be notified from time to time. Issue of
demand notice is prerequisite under Rule 44 or 45 of SVAT 2005 for initiating the
realisation/recovery process against any dealer.

Test-check of records (February-March 2013) of the Commercial Tax Division, Gangtok
for the period from May 2007 to March 2012, revealed that the Division had not
systemically monitored the legitimate use of Way Bills by the dealers. From the records,
it was seen that the Division detected (April 2008) irregular utilisation of Way Bills
towards purchase of iron, steel and cement, not directly involved in usual course of its
business, which was to manufacture medicines and cosmetics, by M/s Golden Cross
Pharma Pvt. Ltd., Rorathang. In response to the related query of the CTD, the company
confirmed that the purchase of construction materials were not related to the
manufacturing process and assured (May 2008) the Division that it shall pay full amount
of the SVAT for all such purchases.

It was, however, seen that despite the earlier detection (April 2008) of evasion of SVAT,
by irregular utilisation of Way Bills, and assurance given by the company to pay the full



amount of tax, the company took inadmissible deductions* while calculating its “taxable
turnover” beyond the period of detection. The company thus, on its continued purchase
of construction materials, kept on evading payment of SVAT. It was further observed
that during the period from May 2007 to March 2012, construction materials worth
% 13.48 crore were purchased by the company without any payment of SVAT. The
Division also had not issued any Demand Notice even for the period up to March 2008,
for which the evasion of SVAT was detected by them.

Thus, inadmissible deductions while calculating its taxable turnover by irregular
utilisation of Way Bills by the company, and lack of follow up and monitoring by the
Division, resulted in evasion and non-recovery of SVAT amounting to % 1.09 crore as
detailed in the Appendix 4.2.

The Division replied (August 2013) that a registered dealer involved in manufacturing
can file way bill for goods imported for use as raw material, packing material, plant,
machinery, consumables and construction material. Hence, the issue of way bill for
import of cement and steel by the dealer was neither irregular nor was there any revenue
loss. The reply is not tenable as the deductions availed by the company pertained to
inter-State transactions of purchase of iron, steel and cement which were not directly
related to the business of the company.

As per Sikkim Value Added Tax (Amendment) Rules 2006 read with Sub-rule (1) and
Sub-rule (2) of Rule 39 of the Sikkim Value Added Tax (SVAT) Rules 2005, in the case
of the works contract where amounts towards labour charges and other like charges or no
non-taxable components, not involving any transfer of property in goods, actually
incurred in connection with the execution of such works contract are not ascertainable,
the State or Central Government or a body making payment of any sums to any
contractor for carrying out such works contract, at the time of payment of such sums in
any manner, shall deduct at source a tax payable under Section 13, at the rate of two per
cent on the gross value of each bill on account of the execution of the works contract.
The paying authority shall issue a certificate in Form 11A to the contractor and a copy
thereof to the appropriate assessing authority, duly verified and signed by the authorised
officer of the paying authority. Further, as per the Rule 42 of the Act ibid every person
entering into any contract with any contractor for execution of works contract, shall
inform the Commissioner of such contract within fifteen days from the date of signing of
the contract or issue of letter of intent. The contractor was also required to file quarterly
and annual returns as per Section 30 of the SVAT Act 2005.

*Inadmissible deduction: The deductions availed by the company were inadmissible as the transactions pertained to the

purchase of iron, steel and cement which were not directly related to the business of the company.



Test check of records revealed (March 2013) that there was no system in place in the
CTD, Gangtok to ensure realisation of tax from the contractors undertaking works of
registered dealers/organisations/bodies in the State through registration of all works
executing contractors, making the works awarding dealers accountable to enforce
realisation from contractors and deposit the same in to the Government account,
obtaining periodical returns along with proof of payment of appropriate tax from the
work awarding entities, appropriate follow up and monitoring etc. It may be mentioned
that in the case of Government departments, such deduction at the source of payment
itself were being ensured by the departmental Drawing and Disbursing Officers.

Scrutiny revealed that there were 422 works contractors registered under CTD, out of
which records relating to only seven were produced. Two firms’ out of seven functioning
as registered works contractors were awarded execution of various works by the Central
Agricultural University at Gangtok. It was further noticed that the works awarding
organisation did not deposit any tax payable by these contractors as required under the
Rules. This organisation also neither informed the CTD of entering into contract with
these contractors for execution of works nor did the Division enquire about the same.
The CTD had not taken any initiative to introduce appropriate system in the Division to
ensure realisation of taxes due from the dealers/organisations/ bodies/ contractors.
Further, the works contractors never filed any quarterly or annual return till the date of
Audit (March 2013).

It was further seen that one works contractor (M/s Supreme Engineering Services, a
Mumbai based contractor), who was not registered, was not paying tax despite the fact
that it was executing various works in the State for pharmaceutical companies (M/s
Golden Cross Pharma Pvt. Ltd and M/s Cipla Ltd). The extent of evasion of tax could
not be quantified due to non-availability of information with the CTD. Ignorance of non-
tegistration of works contractors functioning in the State also indicated that the
prevailing system of ensuring realisation of taxes from works contractors was inadequate
with consequential serious risk of evasion of tax. The Division also confirmed (June
2013) the non-payment of taxes by these works contractors.

Thus, due to systemic inadequacy in the CTD in ensuring realisation of taxes, the
Government could not realise ₹ 38.21 lakh as detailed in Appendix 4.3.

The matter was reported to the Division/Government (May 2013); their reply has not
been received (October 2013).

Audit process starts with the assessment of risks faced by various departments of
Government based on expenditure incurred, criticality/complexity of activities, level of
delegated financial powers, assessment of overall internal controls, etc.

After completion of audit of each unit on a test-check basis, Inspection Reports
containing audit findings are issued to the heads of the departments. The departments are
to furnish replies to the audit findings within one month of receipt of the Inspection
Reports. Whenever replies are received, audit findings are either settled based on
reply/action taken or further action is required by the audited unit for compliance. Some
of the important audit observations arising out of these Inspection Reports are processed



for inclusion in the Audit Reports, which are submitted to the Governor of the State under
Article 151 of the Constitution of India for laying on the table of the Legislature.

The test audits were conducted involving expenditure of € 379.32 crore (including
expenditure of € 338.10 crore of previous years) (details of year-wise break-up is given in
Appendix 5.1) of the State Government under General Sector. This Chapter contains two
Performance Audits on ‘Disaster Management’ and ‘Roads & Bridges Projects funded
under NLCPR and NEC’ as given below:

The State has experienced many earthquakes due to its location in an earthquake prone
zone. During the last 100 years, the State has been hit by 104 recorded cases of
earthquakes of intensity in the range of 3.0 to 8.7 on the Richter scale, translating to an
average of one earthquake per year. These earthquakes, combined with heavy annual
precipitation and landslides, have time and again resulted in loss of life and property.
The GOI provided assistance of ® 200.38 crore for immediate relief and accorded
sanction of € 1,000 crore for long-term reconstruction of damaged infrastructure.

Audit showed that the State, despite being located in a seismically active zone and being a
victim of recurrent natural disasters, was yet to adequately recognise these disasters as
threats which thwarted its developmental plans and mission to transform itself into a
model State within a targeted time frame. The Disaster Management Act 2005 and other
guidelines issued by the GOI from time to time covering all issues of Disaster
Management (DM) had not been implemented fully. The institutional mechanism to
address DM issues had not been firmly established and the DM policy 2007 not fully
implemented. Further, the State DM plans required strengthening and the Departmental
DM plans were not made till date of audit (September 2013). There had been diversion
